deep.reconstruction:
Context: this page belongs to Riemann's student essay 'Versuch einer allgemeinen Auffassung der Integration und Differentiation' (dated 1847). It was printed posthumously in the Gesammelte Werke (1876, ed. Weber/Dedekind). Notation: Π(s)=Γ(s+1) (Gauss). ∂_x^ν z (later 𝔇_x^ν z) is the ν-th 'Ableitung' (derivative of arbitrary order). On p.24/25 it was defined through the generalized Taylor series (formula 2):
z(x+h) = Σ_{n∈Z} h^{ν+n}/Π(ν+n) · ∂_x^{ν+n} z,
with negative-order terms read as repeated integrals. This leads to the Riemann–Liouville form
∂_x^ν z = 1/Π(-ν-1) ∫_k^x (x-t)^{-ν-1} z(t) dt + C^ν,
where the 'complementary function' C^ν is built from arbitrary constants k, K, K_1, ... (for example terms K_n x^{m-n}/Π(m-n) in formula 3).

(a) Definition. Values of ∂_x^ν z and ∂_x^μ z in which all the arbitrary constants k, K, K_1, ... are the same are called 'corresponding values' (correspondirende Werthe). All values belonging to one and the same expansion of z(x+h) are corresponding.

(b) Footnote 1 (note to p.24). An equivalent definition is
∂_x^ν z = Σ_{n=0}^∞ z^{(n)}(k) (x-k)^{n-ν}/Γ(n-ν+1) + C^ν.
Riemann says it is identical with the given one and would contain all values. He nevertheless prefers the chosen form because of its greater flexibility ('Geschmeidigkeit').
Implicit step (mine): expand z(t)=Σ z^{(n)}(k)(t-k)^n/n! and integrate term by term. The Beta integral gives
1/Γ(-ν) ∫_k^x (x-t)^{-ν-1}(t-k)^n dt = n!/Γ(n-ν+1) · (x-k)^{n-ν},
which yields the series.

(c) Footnote 2 (note to p.25). Does the general formula contain all solutions of equation 2? That holds exactly when the functions C are the only functions w which, substituted for ∂_x^ν z, make the series in 2 vanish identically. That is the homogeneous problem
Σ_{n∈Z} h^{ν+n}/Π(ν+n) D^n w = 0.
Riemann states that one can show without difficulty that no algebraic function of x not contained in C does this. He admits he could not decide whether any function at all (beyond C) satisfies the condition.

(d) The last line announces the next topic: computing derivatives of specific functions, beginning with x^μ on the next page.
errors: No outright error on this page. The claim that the series in note 1 is 'identical' with the integral definition requires z to be analytic at k and the Taylor series to converge on the segment [k,x]. Riemann does not state this hypothesis.
The claim that no algebraic function outside C annihilates series 2 is asserted without proof ('ohne Schwierigkeit').

Implicit issue (my analysis): the bilateral series 2, applied to a complementary term such as x^{-ν-m}, generally does not converge in both directions at once. Example: ν=1/2, m=1 gives a bilateral geometric series in (-h/x). It vanishes only formally, e.g. by summing each half via analytic continuation. So 'making series 2 zero' is not well posed without a summation convention. This is part of the known later criticism of Riemann's complementary function (Cayley 1880).
Riemann himself flags the completeness question as open, so the page contains an honest gap rather than an error.

results.what: Representation of the fractional derivative/integral of an analytic function as a term-by-term series Σ z^{(n)}(k)(x-k)^{n-ν}/Γ(n-ν+1), plus complementary function
results.modern_name: Riemann–Liouville fractional derivative applied to a Taylor series (term-by-term fractional differentiation)
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (1847 essay, publ. 1876); related ideas in Liouville (1832)

results.what: Notion of 'corresponding values': values of derivatives of different orders sharing the same arbitrary constants
results.modern_name: Consistent choice of lower terminal and complementary function (semigroup consistency of fractional operators)

results.what: Open question whether the complementary functions C exhaust all solutions of the homogeneous bilateral Taylor series equation; claim that no algebraic function outside C works
results.modern_name: Complementary function problem in Riemann's fractional calculus; bilateral (Riemann–Hardy) Taylor series
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann; later discussed by Cayley (1880) and Hardy (1945, 'Riemann's form of Taylor's series')

deep.surprise_reason: This is a page of Riemann's 1847 student essay on fractional integration and differentiation, published in his Werke (1876). Its footnotes on the series definition and on the complementary-function question are part of that known text.

checkable.sympy: from sympy import *; x,t=symbols('x t',positive=True); nu=Rational(-1,2); n=2; simplify(integrate((x-t)**(-nu-1)*t**n,(t,0,x))/gamma(-nu) - gamma(n+1)/gamma(n-nu+1)*x**(n-nu))
checkable.asserts: Term-by-term step behind note 1 (k=0, ν=-1/2, n=2): the Riemann–Liouville integral of t^n equals n!/Γ(n-ν+1)·x^{n-ν}. Should return 0.
Note-1 series for z=e^x, k=0, ν=-1/2 gives Σ x^{n+1/2}/Γ(n+3/2). This equals the RL half-integral e^x·erf(√x). Numerically ≈ 0.

checkable.sympy: from sympy import *; x=symbols('x',positive=True); nu=Rational(-1,2); simplify(integrate((x-symbols('t'))**(-nu-1)*exp(symbols('t')),(symbols('t'),0,x))/gamma(-nu) - exp(x)*erf(sqrt(x)))
checkable.asserts: The integral form of the definition gives the same value as the series form in note 1 (identity of the two definitions for e^x).

checkable.sympy: from sympy import *; j=symbols('j',integer=True); r=symbols('r',positive=True); simplify(Sum((-r)**j,(j,0,oo)).doit().subs(r,Rational(1,2)) + Sum((-1/r)**j,(j,1,oo)).doit().subs(r,3))
checkable.asserts: Illustration of the convergence caveat: the two halves of the bilateral series for a complementary term converge in disjoint regions (r<1 vs r>1). Their analytic continuations, 1/(1+r) and -1/(1+r), cancel only formally.

transcription_corrections: First line: the red interlinear insertion above 'k, K, ee' reads 'k, k_1, etc. etc.', clarifying the list of constants.
In note 1 the derivative was corrected from a different letter to z: (d^n z/dx^n)_k. The original notation ^x∂^ν_z is struck through on the page and replaced (red) by the later 𝔇/∂ notation.

Margin: the first red note '𝔇_x^ν z ∂_x^ν z) xx) (zu Seite 24) Note unter dem Text' marks note 1 as the footnote xx) to p.24. The second, 'xxx) Note unter dem Text (zu Seite 25) ∂_x^ν z 𝔇_x^ν z', marks note 2 as footnote xxx) to p.25.
In note 2, 'Functionen C' appears as 'Functionen C' with C written like the symbol C^ν. Also 'von' before 'x' in the penultimate line of the box is struck out, consistent with the transcription.
